segments.title: Russian destroyer labels versus actual roles
segments.body: Imperial Russian ship lists contain many vessels built as torpedo boats and later reclassified as destroyers. A new name did not give them the ability to perform destroyer duties: a vessel dominated by torpedoes and carrying only a couple of guns remained a torpedo boat. Russia had a strong reason to want destroyers because its geographically separated fleets had little prospect of mutual support. During the Russo-Japanese War, the supporting fleet arrived after the original fleet had already ceased to be an effective fighting force.

evidence.note: Imperial Russia reclassified many torpedo boats as destroyers even though the new label did not give them the guns or capabilities required for that role.
The discussion ties the need for destroyers to Russia's separated fleets and says a torpedo-dominated craft with too few guns remains a torpedo boat.

segments.summary: Russia needed destroyers for fleets with little prospect of mutual support, while later reclassifications overstated the capability of its torpedo boats.

segments.title: Why torpedo-boat leaders were destroyers
segments.body: Torpedo-boat leaders were destroyers in the period under discussion. The displacement difference between a torpedo boat and a destroyer was often small, so the distinction depended mainly on guns and the ability to engage enemy counterparts. Destroyers soon developed from hunting torpedo boats to fighting other destroyers, a change linked to the large numbers being built. A ship capable of defeating a rival destroyer could probably also defeat a torpedo boat.

evidence.note: Torpedo-boat leaders in this period were destroyers because their gun armament let them hunt torpedo boats and rival destroyers.

segments.summary: Gun armament and the ability to hunt enemy torpedo craft made a torpedo-boat leader a destroyer in this period.
segments.question: Why did navies not build torpedo-boat leaders instead of destroyers?
segments.answerShort: A torpedo-boat leader with enough guns to hunt enemy torpedo craft was effectively a destroyer in this period.

segments.title: Sokol combined destroyer armament with 29-knot speed
segments.body: Sokol was ordered from Yarrow and had the armament and speed expected of a destroyer. She carried one 75 mm gun and three 47 mm guns, alongside two 15-inch torpedo tubes with six torpedoes and capacity for ten mines. Her 29-knot speed was impressive for a ship laid down in 1894 and launched and commissioned in 1895. She survived long enough to join the Bolsheviks in 1917, by which time she had been renamed.

evidence.note: Sokol's Yarrow origin, armament, dates, speed and 1917 allegiance are stated. Six torpedoes explicitly corrects sixteen. The later name is unclear in the captions and is not reconstructed.

segments.summary: Yarrow-built Sokol carried guns, torpedoes, and mines while reaching 29 knots in the mid-1890s.

segments.title: Buinyi's gun positions limited its destroyer role
segments.body: The Buinyi class theoretically carried five 47 mm guns, yet their positions were difficult to crew at operating speed and likely to become very wet. Moving torpedoes around the deck to reload the launchers would make those guns still harder to use during tactical maneuvering. The aft gun was probably the most usable. This was a well-armed torpedo boat whose layout left it poorly suited to destroyer duties. The class fought the Russo-Japanese War as torpedo boats and received the destroyer classification in 1907. Its gun armament was only slightly stronger than Sokol's despite the decade between them, while destroyers elsewhere had grown heavier and the small Hotchkiss guns were becoming weak.

evidence.note: Explains wet gun positions and deck reloading, tentatively identifies the aft gun as most usable, dates reclassification to 1907, and compares the small guns with evolving destroyer armament.

segments.summary: Exposed gun positions and torpedo reloading limited Buinyi's fighting ability, and its destroyer classification came after the Russo-Japanese War.

segments.title: Prestige could not close Russia's capability gap
segments.body: Russia wanted the status of a leading naval power, while its spending priorities, technology, and industrial capacity placed it behind several faster-moving fleets. Germany was ahead, France was probably ahead, and Japan was advancing in technology acquisition. Italy also supplied a relevant comparison. The Royal Navy's technological profile and procurement pace operated at a substantially different scale.

evidence.note: Contrasts Russia's desired status with spending, technology and industry. France is described as probably ahead, and Britain's procurement pace is treated as being on a different scale.

segments.summary: Comparisons with Germany, France, Japan, Italy, and Britain show how Russia's great-power image ran ahead of its naval technology and procurement pace.

segments.title: Stronger rival navies strained Britain's two-power standard
segments.body: Britain's traditional two-power standard used France and Russia as its benchmark. Russia usually formed the smaller addition to the French fleet. Maintaining that margin became harder when the next two naval powers were larger and more effectively supplied, funded, and organized. The practical cost of the standard therefore depended on the strength and support of the fleets being counted.

evidence.note: Explains Russia's relatively small contribution to the traditional France-plus-Russia benchmark and why stronger rival fleets made the two-power standard harder to maintain.

segments.summary: A France-plus-Russia benchmark became harder to sustain as Britain's leading naval rivals grew stronger and better supported.

segments.title: Tsushima exposed Russia's screening shortfall
segments.body: Rozhestvensky's first and second destroyer divisions consisted largely of the Buinyi class and closely related ships. Buinyi could make 26.7 knots and about 1,200 miles at 12 knots, yet the Imperial Russian Navy still classified her type as large torpedo boats during the war. The screen at Tsushima needed gun-armed ships that could keep Japanese torpedo craft away from the battle line. The reported sea state would have limited the guns of any contemporary destroyer, although some designs would have coped much better than others. The Russian vessels' torpedo-focused layouts left their guns particularly difficult to operate. Later references that call these formations destroyer divisions apply the 1907 classification to ships that fought the 1905 battle as torpedo boats.

evidence.note: Buinyi could make 26.7 knots and about 1,200 miles at 12 knots, and ships of her class or closely related types formed most of Rozhestvensky's first and second destroyer divisions.

Explains the need to repel Japanese torpedo craft and acknowledges that the sea state would limit all contemporary destroyers, with gun placement leaving some designs much better off. Later destroyer labels reflect the 1907 reclassification.

segments.summary: At Tsushima, Russia needed destroyers to hold Japanese torpedo craft at bay and arrived with large torpedo boats whose guns were hard to use at sea.

segments.title: Ukrainets showed what a capable Russian destroyer could carry
segments.body: The Ukrainets group carried two 3-inch guns, one forward and one aft, plus four 57 mm guns and more stable torpedo arrangements. The torpedo alternatives given are two 17.7-inch torpedoes or three 15-inch torpedoes, and the ships could make 26 knots. Their larger hulls distinguished them from earlier Russian torpedo craft of roughly 300-450 tons. Public donations funded eight ships, some named after their donors. Although described as completed in 1905, they represented the kind of capable destroyer Russia needed to bring into service earlier. Russia initially called these ships torpedo cruisers and reclassified them as destroyers in 1907, even though their capabilities already suited destroyer duties.

evidence.note: Gives 1905 completion, 26-knot speed, guns and alternative torpedo outfits, larger hulls, eight publicly funded ships and torpedo-cruiser classification before 1907. The 1906 completion date belongs to the next design.

segments.summary: Eight publicly funded Ukrainets ships combined stronger guns and more stable torpedo arrangements, although Russia needed that capability earlier.

segments.title: German-influenced destroyers missed Tsushima
segments.body: The next design shows German influence, compared with the British ideas visible in Ukrainets. A hull of more than 600 tons carried two 75 mm guns, six 57 mm guns, four 7.62 mm machine guns, and three 17.7-inch torpedo tubes. The example given was laid down in 1904 and launched that December, yet did not enter service until 1906. Such ships would have supplied useful destroyer capability at Tsushima if they could have been made ready in time. The suggestion that someone deliberately kept valuable new ships back from a voyage expected to end in defeat remains speculative. Their gun armament and speed later made them useful in World War I.

evidence.note: Contrasts British and German design influence, lists armament and a 1904 launch with 1906 service entry, then speculates about holding useful ships back. Class and ship names fluctuate in the captions, including Borodinsky, so no additional confident identity is supplied.

segments.summary: German design influence produced heavily armed destroyers, while late completion and a speculative decision to hold ships back frame their absence at Tsushima.

segments.title: Outnumbered Russian fleets needed destroyer gunpower
segments.body: Russian fleets were likely to fight outnumbered wherever they operated. Their skirmishing forces therefore had substantial defensive work alongside offensive action. Enemy torpedo boats and destroyers made properly armed destroyers a sensible requirement. Russia nevertheless failed to build enough of them, have them ready, or use them when the opportunity arose.

evidence.note: Explains why outnumbered Russian fleets needed destroyers for defensive as well as offensive work, then criticizes inadequate construction, readiness and use.

segments.summary: Russian skirmishing forces needed to defeat enemy torpedo craft while protecting fleets likely to fight outnumbered.

segments.title: Russian procurement struggled with industry and distant authority
segments.body: Russian planners knew which capabilities they wanted, yet the ships purchased did not consistently deliver them. Some designs exceeded domestic construction capacity, while others could be built only in insufficient numbers. Funding also had to cover bases alongside the desired ships. Procurement suffered from corruption and money directed away from operational needs. The reasons for that recurring corruption remain uncertain. One suggested explanation is that Russia's widely dispersed armed forces operated far from central authority, allowing commanders to treat their responsibilities as personal fiefdoms.

evidence.note: Explains industrial limits and competing expenditure on ships and bases. The proposed link between corruption and forces distant from central authority is explicitly uncertain.

segments.summary: Construction limits and competing demands for ships and bases obstructed procurement; distance from central authority offers a tentative explanation for corruption.

segments.title: Firepower depended on its supporting systems
segments.body: A weapon's purchase price says little about whether it can deliver fire where required. Sensors must identify where to direct it, logistics must supply it, and personnel must operate and support it. Those enablers have to be available before nominal firepower becomes an operational capability. The useful measure is the ability to deploy and sustain that firepower at the required place and time.

evidence.note: Explains sensors, logistics, crews and sustainment as necessary enablers of firepower rather than judging procurement by weapon output alone.

segments.summary: Measuring weapons for the money leaves out the support needed to direct, deploy, and sustain their firepower.

segments.title: British regimental recruitment tied command to responsibility
segments.body: Russia was far from the only state to mismanage military funds. Distance from central authority could be measured in communication time as well as miles, and personal recruitment introduced further opportunities for abuse. British governments came to distrust privately raised regiments, although the concern was not that large numbers existed only on paper. The person who raised a regiment traditionally commanded it in battle, giving him a direct incentive to recruit enough soldiers to survive and perform his task. Recruiting and second battalions nevertheless remained a recurring administrative problem.

evidence.note: Compares military mismanagement across states and explains the recruitment incentive when a regiment's raiser commanded it. Explicitly rejects large numbers of British paper regiments as the explanation for government distrust.

segments.summary: Giving a regiment's recruiter its battlefield command encouraged him to supply real soldiers, although recruiting battalions still developed administrative problems.

segments.title: Why did Britain have so many one-battalion regiments?
segments.body: Britain's history of one-battalion regiments is linked to recurring administrative trouble in second battalions. That experience provides an explanation for retaining a single battalion. The criticism concerns administration rather than fighting ability. Second battalions could still be very good fighters.

evidence.note: Recounts a received question about Britain's one-battalion regiments and answers it with administrative problems in second battalions, explicitly preserving their good fighting quality.

segments.summary: Administrative difficulties in second battalions help explain Britain's one-battalion tradition, despite those battalions' good fighting ability.
segments.question: Why did Britain have so many one-battalion regiments?
segments.answerShort: Recurring administrative problems in second battalions help explain that tradition, even though those battalions could fight very well.

segments.title: Four-ship orders exposed Russia's rebuilding limits
segments.body: Later alterations included 4-inch guns, 1.5-inch anti-aircraft guns, and fittings to carry 25 mines, despite the class comprising only four ships. Their original machinery combined Schultz-Schichau boilers with triple-expansion engines producing 6,500 indicated horsepower for 25 knots. Armament included two 3-inch guns, six 57 mm guns, four 7.62 mm machine guns, and three 17.7-inch torpedo tubes. The ships were well armed and capable of their intended work, although slow beside contemporary destroyers. A four-ship order was inadequate for a major power rebuilding after the Russo-Japanese War.

evidence.note: Gives later armament and mine variants, original machinery and weapons, 25-knot speed and a four-ship order criticized as inadequate. The class name is garbled in the captions and is not reconstructed.

segments.summary: A capable but slow class of four shows why respectable specifications could not rebuild the destroyer force after the Russo-Japanese War.

segments.title: Tsushima's upset belongs beside Trafalgar and Lissa
segments.body: Tsushima belongs beside Lissa and Trafalgar because a large part of one fleet was destroyed and the result changed expectations about naval power. The Japanese performance may even compare favorably with Britain's at Trafalgar. Later dismissals of the Russian Navy can obscure how the contest looked beforehand. Russia entered as a recognized major power, while Japan had not yet received that status, so the paper balance did not predict the outcome.

evidence.note: The transcript groups Tsushima with Lissa and Trafalgar, compares the Japanese performance favorably with Trafalgar, and contrasts Russia's major-power status with Japan's pre-battle standing.

segments.summary: Tsushima's place among decisive naval battles comes from the destruction inflicted and the reversal of prewar expectations about Russia and Japan.

segments.title: Torpedo arcs took priority over usable gun positions
segments.body: Narrowing the forecastle allowed the wing guns to fire forward. The resulting positions were extremely wet and difficult to work at high speed; accounts relayed through translations of Russian documents suggest that description understated how dangerous and impractical they were. Raising the guns and widening the forecastle offered a way to improve their serviceability, although it might restrict torpedo firing arcs. A destroyer needed guns that were as usable as its torpedoes. Accepting poor gun positions to preserve torpedo arcs indicated the priorities of a torpedo boat.

evidence.note: Explains the narrowed forecastle, wet gun positions and the alternative of raising guns, with a possible cost to torpedo arcs. The assessment of crew danger is relayed from people translating Russian documents.

segments.summary: A narrowed forecastle gave wing guns forward fire while exposing their crews to water, revealing the priority assigned to torpedoes.

segments.title: Helicopter facilities revealed a ship's anti-submarine priority
segments.body: The space and support assigned to equipment reveal what a warship is expected to do. In an anti-submarine ship, helicopter facilities and the flight deck might occupy about a third of the vessel, leaving less room for missiles and guns. A ship can consequently appear lightly armed because so much of its volume supports aviation. Placing weapons above the hangar may require arrangements that reduce its height or otherwise limit helicopter facilities. Preserving that space is a deliberate mission choice, and the same attention to equipment arrangement helps distinguish early destroyers from torpedo boats.

evidence.note: Uses a hypothetical anti-submarine ship whose aviation facilities occupy about 30 percent or a third of the ship, including the hangar-height cost of weapons above it, to show how layout reveals mission priorities.

segments.summary: Hangar volume, flight decks, and helicopter support can consume enough space to determine which other weapons a ship can carry.

segments.title: Larger destroyers still brought limited range and new machinery
segments.body: The follow-on ships were presented as enlarged and improved versions of the Ukrainets group, although they were slower. Their outfit included more machine guns and three 17.7-inch torpedo tubes; the comparison with the earlier class's tubes is explicitly uncertain. French Normand boilers added another machinery origin after German, British, Russian, and Swiss choices, complicating maintenance and training. Triple-expansion engines produced 7,300 indicated horsepower for 25 knots. Their best-case range was about 2,400 nautical miles at 12 knots, which was disappointing for a roughly 700-ton design that might have benefited from the lessons of the Tsushima voyage. Only four were built, with the last completed in September 1907.

evidence.note: Describes enlarged Ukrainets successors, uncertain comparison of torpedo outfits, Normand boilers, 7,300 ihp, 25 knots, best-case 2,400-nautical-mile range and four ships completed by September 1907. Class names are garbled and are not reconstructed.

segments.summary: An enlarged follow-on design carried stronger torpedo armament, yet its speed, range, machinery variety, and four-ship order limited the improvement.

segments.title: Machinery variety weakened Russia's deterrent image
segments.body: The destroyers were capable ships for their period, yet repeated changes of boilers and engines burdened the force supporting them. Great powers needed to project strength, and a strong image required practical capability behind it. Specialists examining the machinery would recognize the inconsistent choices as a logistics weakness. People judging by outward appearance were more likely to notice ship numbers, guns, and torpedoes. Different engines therefore brought little benefit to that public image while exposing weakness to informed observers.

evidence.note: Contrasts naval specialists who recognize machinery variety as a support weakness with observers impressed by numbers and visible weapons. The public-image explanation continues after 37:12.

segments.summary: Distinctive machinery offered little public prestige while making Russia's support problems conspicuous to naval specialists.

segments.title: Lieutenant Shestakov combined heavy armament with limited speed
segments.body: The Lieutenant Shestakov class enlarged a German-built design for domestic construction and began as torpedo cruisers before receiving the destroyer designation. Cutouts in the superstructure kept the wing guns at a low level despite the raised forecastle. Triple-expansion machinery and Normand boilers gave a stated range of 1,994 nautical miles at 12 knots, but extensive reworking failed to achieve the designed 25 knots. The best reported trial figure was 24.78 knots, a claim treated as probably credible because it admitted such a small shortfall. Later armament changes introduced two 120 mm guns, removed the 75 mm battery, added two 47 mm anti-aircraft guns, and increased mine capacity. Whether the revised weapon balance moved these ships back toward torpedo-boat duties remains uncertain. They joined the Black Sea Fleet's torpedo brigade and were considered more than adequate for likely Ottoman opponents. Only four were built.

evidence.note: Describes domestic enlargement, low wing-gun cutouts, Normand boilers, triple-expansion engines, stated range and a reported 24.78-knot trial result treated as probably credible. The original gun tally conflicts with the later tally and is not presented as settled.
Describes rearmament and doubts about its effect on the gun-torpedo balance, Black Sea torpedo-brigade service, likely Ottoman opponents and only four ships.

segments.summary: The Lieutenant Shestakov class gives a Black Sea example of heavy destroyer firepower offset by speed limits and a four-ship production run.

segments.title: Novik combined turbine speed with a heavy destroyer armament
segments.body: Designed by Vulkan-Werke, Novik displaced 1,280 tons normally and 1,620 tons fully loaded, making her substantially larger than the earlier destroyers discussed. Her 37.3 knots on trials became about 36 knots in practice, and she could cover 2,000 nautical miles at 21 knots. Six water-tube boilers supplied turbines driving three shafts. Four single 4-inch guns, four twin 18-inch torpedo mountings, and capacity for 60 mines gave her a powerful armament.

evidence.note: Gives Vulkan-Werke design, displacement, trial and practical speeds, stated range, boilers, three turbine-driven shafts, guns, torpedo mountings and mines.

segments.summary: Novik combined roughly 36 knots in practice with substantial guns, torpedoes, mine capacity, and a 2,000-nautical-mile range at 21 knots.

segments.title: Novik's descendants reached service across a prolonged programme
segments.body: The wider Novik family numbered 53 ships, but some were not built until 1925. Novik herself was laid down in 1910, launched in 1911, and commissioned in 1913. The Derzky group followed with launches between October 1913 and July 1914, and many descendants later served with the Soviet Navy. One Black Sea example left Russia with Wrangel's fleet, was interned at Bizerte in Tunisia, and was scrapped in 1924. Another is described as among the first Soviet naval ships sunk by a Stuka dive bomber. Individual ships had useful speed and power, but the prolonged programme failed to deliver the required force soon enough.

evidence.note: States the family count and delayed completion, Novik's construction dates, Derzky launches and later service. Names of the ships associated with Wrangel and the Stuka sinking are garbled in the captions, so those identities remain unspecified.

segments.summary: A 53-ship family stretched into 1925, with descendants serving the Soviet Navy or leaving Russia with Wrangel's fleet.

segments.title: Four separated fleets required far more destroyers
segments.body: Russia's Black Sea, Baltic, Pacific, and northern naval forces each had to survive and operate on their own. Calling a force a squadron or flotilla did not remove its need for the capabilities of a functioning fleet. The proposed minimum was three or four destroyer divisions in each area, put at 24 to 32 ships per fleet. Financial limitations were real, and public subscriptions helped fund some vessels. Russia nevertheless possessed extensive natural resources and considerable wealth. Poor allocation and spending prevented those resources from supplying enough destroyers for the separate fleets.

evidence.note: Explains four fleets' independent requirements, proposes 24 to 32 destroyers per fleet, acknowledges financial limits and public subscriptions, and distinguishes resource wealth from allocation.

segments.summary: Russia's separated naval forces each needed a substantial destroyer establishment, with 24 to 32 ships per fleet proposed as a minimum.

segments.title: Destroyer crews benefited from close cooperation
segments.body: Destroyer officers and ratings had to work closely together in cramped ships, which encouraged practical cooperation. Torpedo boats and destroyers offered little of the prestige sought by politically connected noble officers, so their commanders could be selected more often for competence. Small crews also had little room for persistent disciplinary trouble and removed men who disrupted the ship. The result could be a well-exercised, motivated, and competently led crew even when Russia had too few destroyers.

evidence.note: Close cooperation between officers and ratings, the low appeal of destroyer service to politically connected officers, and the discipline and repeated practice demanded by compact crews could produce capable Russian destroyer teams.

segments.summary: Russian destroyers could attract competent officers and cohesive crews because small-ship service demanded close cooperation and offered little aristocratic prestige.

segments.title: The Orfey subclass remained a useful destroyer
segments.body: The Orfey subclass carried nine torpedo launchers in three triple mountings, compared with Novik's eight tubes in four twin mountings. The ships retained 4-inch guns and machine guns, with capacity for 18 naval mines. Two steam turbines drove two shafts and gave a speed of about 31 knots. This combination made the subclass useful for destroyer duties.

evidence.note: The useful Orfey design combined nine torpedo launchers, 4-inch guns, space for eighteen mines, 31-knot speed, and twin-shaft turbine machinery.

segments.summary: The Orfey branch of the Novik family combined turbine propulsion, 4-inch guns, nine torpedo launchers, mine capacity, and 31-knot speed.

segments.title: Naval infrastructure could strengthen Russia's wider economy
segments.body: Russia could build useful destroyers, but needed them after Tsushima and before World War I. Supporting its separated fleets also required investment in ports and the railways connecting them with the capital and interior. Those links could strengthen the wider economy by moving goods as well as naval supplies. Arctic supply routes were less practical during World War I than during World War II, and routes across Siberia offered another way to bring goods into Russia. Russia extracted abundant raw materials but lacked enough successive layers of industrial production to be self-sufficient. Later Soviet economic plans sought to develop that industrial capacity. World War I exposed the weakness when imports through the Baltic and Black Sea ports were cut off.

evidence.note: Connects naval investment to ports and railways, compares Arctic and Siberian supply possibilities, and explains raw materials without sufficient industrial depth. Links Soviet industrial plans to weaknesses exposed by restricted wartime imports.

segments.summary: Investment in fleet bases and railways could improve Russia's transport network and address industrial weaknesses exposed by wartime import restrictions.

segments.title: Baltic destroyers could preserve Swedish supply routes
segments.body: More destroyers in the Baltic could have supported convoys across to neutral Sweden. The railway from Narvik into Sweden offered a possible connecting route for imported goods. Chartering neutral shipping was another option. These possibilities depended on having enough suitable ships and being able to maintain the crossing. They offered no assurance that Russia would survive World War I, but the shortage of destroyers removed options before they could be tried.

evidence.note: Proposes Baltic convoys to neutral Sweden and the Narvik railway, or chartering neutral ships, while explicitly refusing to promise that these measures would succeed or ensure Russian survival.

segments.summary: Convoys to Sweden, its rail connection with Narvik, and chartered neutral ships offered possible supply routes without guaranteeing Russia's survival.

segments.title: What if Russia had built balanced destroyers earlier?
segments.body: The closing question asks what would happen if Russia invested consistently in proper destroyers from the beginning. Its early strong start gave way to vessels treated here as torpedo boats before capable destroyers returned later. The proposed alternative keeps building ships that balance gun power with torpedo capability. Larger hulls and longer range would suit the considerable distances Russian ships had to travel. The audience is invited to consider the consequences, and the question remains unanswered.

evidence.note: The transcript asks viewers how Russian history might change if the navy kept building larger, long-range destroyers that balanced guns and torpedoes.

segments.summary: The closing counterfactual asks what consistent investment in larger, longer-range destroyers would have changed from the beginning of Russia's destroyer programme.

segments.title: Towing torpedo craft to Tsushima reduced training
segments.body: Most of the vessels called destroyers at Tsushima required towing and support on the voyage because they could not carry enough fuel. Time under tow prevented normal maneuvering, steaming, and gunnery practice. Releasing them for occasional drills did not reproduce the continuous experience available to ships steaming independently. Towing also constrained the ships towing them, which could not execute battle maneuvers without risking the tow.

evidence.note: Many Russian torpedo craft needed towing or support on the voyage to Tsushima, limiting manoeuvring and steaming practice for both the towed vessels and their escorts.

segments.summary: Short-ranged Russian torpedo craft needed towing and support on the voyage to Tsushima, restricting realistic drills for the towed ships and their escorts.
